explanations.explanation: Right there in verse 1: "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands." The sky is not just sitting up there looking pretty. It's pointing at the One who made it. Friend, that's the best sign anybody ever hung over a bakery, and it's free for everyone.

David doesn't say wrath anywhere in this verse. He says the heavens declare God's glory and the skies proclaim the work of His hands. I think he's standing there with his head tipped back, taking in something wonderful. Nobody looks at a sky full of stars and says, "Hoo, somebody's in trouble."

No kings show up in this verse at all. What the heavens declare is the glory of God, and the skies proclaim the work of His hands. The sky isn't handing out royal gossip, friend. It's got a much bigger story to tell.

explanations.answer: Day after day and night after night
explanations.explanation: David says, "Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge." That's a sky that never takes a day off. No weekends, no holidays, no sick days. I'd love that work ethic on a Monday morning.

David never limits it to one day. He says the speech pours forth "Day after day…" So the sky isn't saving its message for a special occasion. It keeps going every single day, and the night shift is covered too.

explanations.answer: Only when the moon is full
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't wait on the moon. David says the sky reveals knowledge "night after night…" and that includes the nights with a skinny little sliver of moon. Full or not, the message keeps coming. It never checks the calendar first.

Verse 3 says it plainly: "Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard…" So the sky speaks, and you can't hear a thing. Friend, that's the quietest sermon ever preached, and its voice still goes out into all the earth (Psalm 19:4).

Thunder is loud, and verse 3 says the opposite. It says "…without a sound to be heard…" David is describing a speech that comes across with no noise at all. It's a lot like how you can walk into a quiet kitchen and just know the cookies are done.

No wind in this verse, friend. David says the speech comes "Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard…" So there's no rush, no rumble, nothing for your ears. The sky gets its point across in total silence.

Verse 4 says their voice "…has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world." All the earth, friend. Not just one town, one people or one bakery. A message with no sound that still reaches the ends of the world has some serious range.

The word isn't temple. David says the voice has gone out into all the earth, and then adds that the words reach "…the ends of the world." That's way bigger than any one building. The sky speaks to everybody, wherever they're standing.

Kingdom is a fair guess, but it isn't David's word. He says the voice has gone out into all the earth, with words reaching "…the ends of the world." No borders, no passports. The sky doesn't stop at any kingdom's edge.

Yes, friend. Verse 5 says the sun is "Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber…" Picture a man stepping out on his wedding day, and now picture the sun doing it every morning. That's a grand entrance, and I wish my entrance to the bakery got that kind of attention.
It's actually true. David says the sun is "Like a bridegroom emerging from his chamber…" in verse 5. Right after that comes a second picture of the sun, a champion. So the answer is True, friend.
David says the sun is "…like a champion rejoicing to run his course…" Rejoicing, friend. That champion is not dragging his feet to the starting line. He's happy to be running.

David's champion isn't resting. He's "…rejoicing to run his course…" The picture is of a runner full of energy at the start, and it matches the sun heading out across the sky. No battle is mentioned in this verse at all.

A king? Bowing? Not in this verse, friend. The champion is "…rejoicing to run his course…" He's not bowing to anybody, he's too busy being glad about the run! That's the picture David uses for the sun taking off across the sky.

Not quite, friend. Verse 6 says the sun "…rises at one end of the heavens and runs its circuit to the other; nothing is deprived of its warmth." Nothing is left out. If you're wondering whether your corner of the world got skipped, David says no.

That's right. David says "nothing is deprived of its warmth." The sun makes its whole run from one end of the heavens to the other, and not one thing gets skipped. Even the spot in the yard where the dog lies down gets covered.
Verse 7 says, "The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul…" Perfect and reviving, friend. It's not a heavy thing that drains you. It's something that brings you back to life.

Testing isn't the word David uses. He says the Law of the LORD is perfect, "…reviving the soul…" That's the opposite of tiring you out. I think anybody who's been running on empty would hear good news in that.
No scales here, friend. David says the Law of the LORD is perfect, "…reviving the soul…" Instead of weighing you down, it lifts you up. That's a very different feeling from a Monday morning.

Verse 8 says, "the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes." Radiant and giving light, friend. It's like somebody finally flipped the switch in a dark room. I spent years in the back of a dark junk drawer, so believe me, light matters.

Rest sounds nice, but it isn't David's word. He says the commandments are "…radiant, giving light to the eyes." Light is what the commandments give. Think of how much easier it is to see where you're going with the lights on.

No tears in this verse. David calls the commandments of the LORD "…radiant, giving light to the eyes." Right before it, he says the precepts of the LORD bring "…joy to the heart…" So the whole feeling here is bright, friend.

Verse 9 says, "The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever…" Forever, friend. Everything else in my kitchen wears out eventually, even my best mixing bowl. David says this one doesn't, because it endures forever.
A lifetime is long, but David goes further. He says the fear of the LORD is pure, "enduring forever." It doesn't stop when a life stops. That's one lasting thing, friend.
A season would be way too short. David says the fear of the LORD is pure, "enduring forever." It doesn't come and go like the weather. It stays.
Careful, friend. Verse 9 says, "the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous." Altogether, not partly. David leaves no room for a half-righteous judgment.
That's right, friend. David says, "the judgments of the LORD are true, being altogether righteous." Altogether! That word doesn't leave a single crumb of "partly" on the counter.

Not at all, friend. David says they are "…more precious than gold, than much pure gold…" and "…sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb." You don't treasure a burden like gold or taste it like honey. Nobody brags about their heavy burden.

That's right. David calls them "…more precious than gold…" and "…sweeter than honey…" Those are things people want, not things people drag around. The picture is of something rich and sweet that David treasures.

Yes, friend. Verse 11 says, "By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward." David says the LORD's words warn him, and that great reward is found in keeping them. That's worth knowing in any kitchen.

It's actually true. David says, "in keeping them is great reward." Right before that, he says that by them "…Your servant is warned…" So the warning comes through the LORD's words, and the great reward is in keeping them.

David asks, "Cleanse me from my hidden faults." He just asked, "Who can discern his own errors?" so he asks God to cleanse the faults he may not even see. That's an honest prayer, friend. I think it's a good one to borrow.

explanations.answer: Show him who his enemies are
explanations.explanation: Enemies aren't in this verse. David asks, "Cleanse me from my hidden faults." He's looking at his own heart, not at anybody else's. It's a humble thing to do.

explanations.answer: Give him more time to fix them
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask for more time. He says, "Cleanse me from my hidden faults." He asks God to do the cleansing, not to wait while he tries on his own. I think that's a relief to hear.
David prays, "Keep Your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me." He doesn't want sin sitting in charge of his life. Friend, that's a prayer worth praying every morning.
Shame isn't in David's prayer. He says, "Keep Your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me." What he doesn't want is for sin to be the boss of him.
Following isn't the word. David prays, "may they not rule over me." The worry is sin sitting on the throne of his life. He asks God to keep him from it.
Yes, friend. David says, "Then I will be blameless and cleansed of great transgression." It follows his prayer for God to keep him from willful sins. It's good news at the end of a serious prayer.

It's true, friend. David says, "Then I will be blameless and cleansed of great transgression." That line comes right after he prays for God to keep him from willful sins. It's a hopeful note, and a good one.

David prays, "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD…" Both the words he says out loud and the thoughts he keeps inside. Friend, that covers everything, even the stuff I mutter at a burnt batch.

True is a good word, but it isn't the one David uses. He prays that his words and the meditation of his heart will be "…pleasing in Your sight, O LORD…" What he's asking for is that God would be pleased with them.

David isn't asking to be remembered. He prays, "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD…" Pleasing is what he's after, in the words he says and the thoughts he holds.
The psalm ends with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." Two names, and David finishes his whole prayer on them. I think that's a strong place to land, friend.

Shepherd and King are good names, friend, but David doesn't use them in this line. He closes with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." That comes right after he asks that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be pleasing in God's sight. A shepherd needs a whole field of sheep, but a rock just sits there and holds, and I'm a stamper who knows how nice that sounds.

Light and Shield sound like a strong team, friend, like a buddy cop movie. But David doesn't use them here. He ends with "…O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer." A rock is something you can stand on, and a redeemer is the One who buys you back. I know a little about being picked up for a quarter, so that last name hits me right in the handle.
